summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Palau. The Penal Code signed by President Tommy Remengesau Jr. in April 2014 and in force since 23 July 2014 contains no offence outlawing consensual sex between people of the same sex. It removed the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment. Before that repeal male same-sex sexual activity was illegal and female same-sex activity was legal. The Attorney General confirmed the repeal to the Human Dignity Trust.

Palau accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts and to combat discrimination at its Universal Periodic Review, and in October 2011 the government promised to fully decriminalise homosexuality. On 22 March 2011 Palau joined the Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries, which called on states to end acts of violence, criminal sanctions and related human rights violations committed against individuals because of sexual orientation or gender identity.

No legal gender recognition procedure, identity-document or marker rule, screening practice, facility rule, custody provision, or gender-affirming care provision specific to transgender people is provided in Palauan law. No transgender-specific penalties, enforcement measures, or protection-machinery outcomes are documented. There are no anti-discrimination laws concerning sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans visitor has no statutory discrimination protection to invoke.

Partner recognition is closed. The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and a trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to marital recognition or to the protections attached to it.

In July 2019 President Remengesau Jr. said he supports striking down the constitutional ban as discriminatory and believes in full equality. No repeal outcome is stated.
tangentialFactors: Palau appeared on a list published around 2011 by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights of more than 70 Pacific and global jurisdictions whose laws still criminalised same-sex relations. Palau and Nauru both accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appearances, a stated commitment to repeal rather than an unannounced change. The 2014 repeal dropped the global count of anti-sodomy jurisdictions to 79.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ residents of Palau do not possess the same legal protections as other residents. There are no anti-discrimination laws concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman. The ban was added in 2008 among 22 amendments passed in the 4 November 2008 referendum. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2011 list of jurisdictions criminalising same-sex relations predates Palau's 2014 repeal and describes the position then in force, not the current one.

President Remengesau Jr.'s July 2019 support for striking the constitutional marriage ban has no stated repeal outcome; whether any amendment process has been initiated is not sourced.

No sourced material describes police or prosecutorial practice, incidents of violence against transgender people, or entry and immigration screening practice in Palau. The absence of transgender-specific legal provisions is documented as an absence of law; it is not evidence about how officials treat trans visitors in practice.
